## Description

Input on the left, send button on the right.
The body beneath the tabs has 8 pixels of padding, on the same flat surface as the selected tab, the ribbon's tab row colour, #333333 in dark mode, untinted by the mode, and joined to the selected tab with no line between them. In it, the text input sits in a dark box on the theme's darkest surface, #111111 in dark mode, with corners rounded 4 pixels and no border, as tall as the column of buttons beside it, 8 pixels from it, and taller when its text needs more. The text sits 8 pixels in from the box's top, left, and right, and grows down through the box. Clicking anywhere in the box beneath the text puts focus in the text, except while a preview shows. The preview shows in the same box, its content inset 8 pixels all round.
At the right, a column of three buttons, 88 pixels wide, 8 pixels apart, each as tall as the input's single row: Send at the top, then Queue, then Preview, each the column's full width, flat, with no border or shadow and corners rounded 2 pixels. Send has a paper-plane send icon before its label, in semibold text, and keeps its split chevron, its menu still offering "Send to task". Queue and Preview are flat buttons on the theme's base surface, #444444 in dark mode, their labels in the theme's text colour, a step lighter on hover, doing what the send menu's options of those names do, with tooltips saying that Queue queues the prompt even while the harness is free, and that Preview previews the compiled prompt. They are offered just as the menu is: both are disabled while the input is empty, while a preview shows, and while a queued prompt is edited, and Queue is also disabled on the Ask tab, since a question never queues.
<Enter> allows for creating new lines, like Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it to the HarnessIntegration
Sending sends the prompt in the selected tab's mode, as the [PromptSending](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says. While the selected tab's lane is busy, as it says, the send button on the Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform tabs reads "Queue", since the prompt will queue: on Code while a task runs in the code lane, on Chain and Spec while one runs in the spec lane, and on Freeform while one runs in either, a Freeform task keeping both busy. Otherwise it reads "Send", so Spec reads "Send" while only a Code task runs. On the Ask tab it always reads "Send", because a question is never queued. The button is only disabled while the input is empty.
On the Code tab, while the send menu offers "Send to task", as its options say, the running task being a Code task in the code lane, the send button reads "Send to task" instead of "Queue", its tooltip saying it sends the prompt to the running task, and it and <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS) send to the task just as that option does, rather than queueing. The Queue button and the menu's "Queue" still queue the prompt. While the code lane is busy any other way, a Freeform task running, a Code task whose harness can't be fed more, a task building or compiling, or the previous tasks expanded over its output, the button reads "Queue" and the prompt queues, as ever. The Chain, Spec, Freeform, and Ask tabs never send to a task this way.

## Instructions

- [ChatInputInstruction](../../../shape/ChatInput.md#chat-input-instruction)

## Send Options

### Split Button

The send button is a split button: the send or queue button itself, and joined to its right, a narrow half with a chevron that opens a menu of other ways to send the prompt, above the button, its right edge lined up with the button's. The chevron half is disabled whenever the send half is, and while a preview shows, and its tooltip says it shows more ways to send, with its shortcut.

### Keyboard

<Ctrl+Shift+Enter> (<Cmd+Shift+Enter> on macOS) in the chat input opens the menu with its first option highlighted, and does nothing while the input is empty or a preview shows. While it is open, the text keeps focus, <Up> and <Down> move the highlight, wrapping around, <Enter> picks the highlighted option, and <Escape> closes the menu, as does pressing <Ctrl+Shift+Enter> again or the mouse anywhere outside it. Each option highlights on hover, and clicking one picks it.
## Tabs

The tabs along the top of the chat input, one for each mode.

### Overview

The input and buttons live inside the body of a tab bar, a flat strip 32 pixels tall on the ribbon's command area colour, #222222 in dark mode, with no line anywhere in it, whether beneath it, between its tabs, or around them. Each tab is only its label, in small text, with 8 pixels to each side of it and no border, and its label is always in its mode's colour at full strength, of the [PromptModes](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes), whether selected or not: Code red, Chain's icon purple, Spec blue, Ask green, and Freeform grey. The one exception is Chain selected, when Code and Spec take Chain's purple too, as the chain says. The selected tab is marked only by its background, the same surface as the body beneath it, so it reads as a tab joined to that body; unselected tabs have none, and show the strip, lightening a little on hover. There is a tab for each of the [PromptModes](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes), in their order: Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, and Freeform. Code, Spec, Ask, and Freeform are ordinary tabs. Chain is also a tab, just a small one, because it only shows an icon. All five sit flush against each other with no extra gaps, and no tab has more padding than a normal tab.
The chat input starts in the combined mode: Chain is selected, so Code and Spec are selected together, and a prompt sent before switching tabs changes the code and the spec together. Each open project keeps the tab it was left on, as the [OpenProjects](../../open-projects/index.md#open-projects) says, so a project starts on Chain the first time it is opened in a launch, and switching back to it selects the tab it was on.
Pressing <Ctrl+Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to Chain to Spec to Ask to Freeform and back to Code, <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> the other way, and focus remains in the chat input. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.
<Tab> and <Shift+Tab> don't switch tabs, and don't indent the text either. They move keyboard focus out of the chat input to the next or previous control, as they do everywhere else. While the completion menu is open, <Tab> is still the menu's.

### Chain

Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it selects both Code and Spec. Its icon is drawn in Chain's colour, the purple of the [PromptModes](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes), selected or not, as every tab's label is in its mode's colour. It never shows a focus outline, and its icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two is selected.
Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of them.
Chain, like every tab, has no line along its bottom or sides, in combined mode or separate, since the tab bar draws no lines at all. Nothing draws a line beneath Chain and then hides it, since a hidden line can show again wherever rounding to the display's pixels uncovers it.
Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both. Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected, Code and Spec both show as selected, one continuous background beneath the two of them and Chain, reading as a single unified tab. Chain itself has a transparent background, so the joined Code and Spec show through underneath it.
While Chain is selected, the Code and Spec labels are drawn in Chain's purple, the same colour as its icon, rather than red and blue, so the unified tab reads as one mode in one colour. Their colour follows the slide: as Code and Spec slide together, their labels shift from red and blue to purple, and as they slide apart they shift back, each reaching its own colour as the tabs settle.

### Help

To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.
It reads what the selected tab's mode is for, as the [PromptModes](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes) says.

### Session

At the far right of the bar, at the right end of the help text, sits how much context the selected tab's conversation holds, then a New conversation button. Each lane's tasks, and the questions of the Ask tab, have a conversation of their own, as the [HarnessIntegration](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says, so the figure is the spec lane's on the Spec and Chain tabs, a Chain prompt starting in the spec lane, the code lane's on Code and Freeform, and the questions' on Ask.
The figure reads "Context", then the number of tokens, short and extra small, muted: "850", "42.1k", "123k", or "1.2M", to a decimal place below a hundred of a unit. It follows each reply as the harness reports it. While the next prompt would start a new conversation, as when the project has none yet or New conversation was just pressed, it reads "Context 0". Its tooltip says how many tokens the conversation the next prompt carries on holds, or that the next prompt starts a new conversation.
New conversation is a small ghost button with a sparkles icon, reading "New conversation". Pressing it starts a new conversation for the selected tab: the spec lane's on Spec, the code lane's on Code and Freeform, both lanes' on Chain, whose steps run in both, and the questions' on Ask. The next run of that conversation, from any tab sharing it, starts a new one with no context instead of carrying on, and the figure reads "Context 0". A run of the conversation left that is still going finishes as it would, but neither it nor the project's history brings that conversation back, even once the project is closed and opened again, as the [HarnessIntegration](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says.
It can be pressed while a run in that conversation is under way, a task on Code, Chain, Spec, or Freeform, or any question on Ask, without waiting for it to finish. Pressed while a task runs, the prompts sent meanwhile queue or run as ever, and the next task of the lane reset to start, whether sent straight away or from the queue, starts a new conversation with no context, the ones after it carrying that one on. That holds even when the running task is the first of its conversation and the harness hasn't yet said which conversation it is: once it does, it isn't carried on either.
Whether a task starts a new conversation is part of its prompt, recorded in its hidden anchor. Pressed for a lane with prompts queued, New conversation marks the first in that lane's queue, saving it again with the project, so it still starts the new conversation once the project is closed and opened again. With nothing queued, the next task sent or queued takes the mark. Cancelling the marked prompt passes the mark on to the one that now comes first, or, with nothing left queued, to the next task sent or queued. A task marked this way never carries on the conversation before it when it runs.
<Ctrl+N> while in the chat input does just what pressing New conversation does, for the selected tab, and nothing while the button is disabled. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.
Its tooltip says which conversation it resets, with its shortcut: "Start a new conversation for spec tasks (Ctrl+N)", "Start a new conversation for code tasks (Ctrl+N)", "Start a new conversation for spec and code tasks (Ctrl+N)", or "Start a new conversation for questions (Ctrl+N)", adding, while a run in it is under way, that the run finishes in the conversation left. It is disabled only while that conversation has nothing to carry on and no run in it is under way, its tooltip then saying the next task, or question, already starts a new conversation.
Both sit on the bar's bottom line, which runs beneath them as it does beneath the help text, and neither is cut off: the help text gives way to them when the bar is narrow.

### Usage

Just right of the context figure, before New conversation, sits the agent's usage: how much of the harness picked, of the [HarnessIntegration](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration), has been used, as Claude Code's /usage shows it. Its summary is short and extra small, muted like the context figure: "Usage", then the share used of the plan limit nearest to running out, such as "Usage 42%", turning the theme's warning colour from 80% and its error colour once the limit is reached. When the harness reports no plan limits, the summary is what this project's runs would cost at API prices, as below, such as "Usage $1.24", or the tokens they used, as the context figure is written, when no cost can be worked out. Until anything has been reported, it reads "Usage", with nothing after it.
Clicking the summary opens a popover above it with all the details, each group headed, and each figure labelled:
- Plan limits: each limit the harness reports, such as the current
  session's and the week's, with the share used as a bar and a
  percentage, and when it resets.
- Conversation: the context the selected tab's conversation holds,
  and its input, output, cache-read, and cache-written tokens, and
  what they would cost at API prices.
- This project: every run the project has made, as below, split
  into tasks and questions, with its tokens by model and what
  they would cost at API prices.
- The harness and model the figures came from, and when they were
  last reported.
The popover is laid out in two columns side by side, with a gap of 16 pixels between them and a thin line in the theme's line colour down the middle. The left column holds what is going on now: Plan limits, then Conversation, then, at its foot, the harness and model the figures came from. The right column holds This project, which is the longest: Tasks and Questions, then the tokens by model, then its cost with its breakdown and the note about API prices. Each column is as tall as its own groups, both starting at the top, and the popover is as tall as the taller of them. Each column is at least 240 pixels wide, so the popover is about twice as wide as it was as one column, but never wider than the window less 16 pixels each side; where the window is too narrow for both, the right column goes beneath the left, as one column again, with no line between them. A column whose groups are all left out is not shown, and the other is the popover's only column; when nothing has been reported at all, the popover is a single column saying so. Within each column, each figure is a row, its label at the left and its value right-aligned in tabular figures. The popover scrolls as a whole, not each column on its own, when it is taller than the room above the summary.
A group, or a figure, the harness doesn't report is left out rather than shown as zero, and when nothing has been reported the popover says so. The figures come from what the harness reports as its runs go, and from what it reported for the runs saved in the project, never from running anything of its own to ask, and update in place while the popover is open, following each reply. Clicking outside the popover, or pressing Escape, closes it. The summary's tooltip says to click for the details. Like the context figure, it is never cut off: the help text gives way to it.
A run's own usage is never the figures its result reports as they stand. Claude Code's result reports its `modelUsage` and `total_cost_usd` as running totals for the whole conversation, so a run that carries on a conversation includes every run before it in that conversation. A run's own figures are how much its conversation's totals rose since that conversation's previous run, each model's tokens apart; a run that carries on a copy of a conversation, as a question asked while another runs does, is measured from the run whose conversation it copied. When the totals went down instead, any of them, the conversation started over, and the run counts in full, as does the first run of a conversation. Runs are taken in the order they were sent, whether they were saved in the history or have just reported, so every run is counted once and no run's figures are counted again in a later one's.
This project covers every run saved with the project, every task in its history, each step of a chain counted as a run of its own, and every question in its asks, not only those since it was opened, worked out from what the harness printed for each, as its record keeps it. It keeps updating as new runs report, each run counted once it reports, and a run under way not yet counted. It is split into Tasks and Questions, each giving how many runs there were and, beside it, muted, how many of them reported no usage, such as "42 runs · 3 without usage", the latter left out when none. Beneath them, for each model the runs used, by name, its input, output, cache-read, and cache-written tokens, as the context figure writes them, across tasks and questions together.
Cost is worked out from the tokens, at each model's published API prices per million tokens, which the application keeps for the models it knows: input, output, cache reads, and cache writes, at the 5-minute rate or the 1-hour rate, using the split between them the harness reports. Cache writes it reports no split for are priced at the 5-minute rate. A model is matched by its id, whatever date or context-size suffix it carries. The cost the harness reports itself, such as `total_cost_usd`, is never used. A model whose prices aren't known gets no cost, never a guess: its tokens are still shown, it is marked "Price unknown", and the totals that leave it out say so beside them. The project's cost is shown as a total, and beneath it how much of it was input, output, cache reads, and cache writes, each in dollars and as a share of the total, since caching is most of it. Beneath the cost, muted, it says this is what the tokens would cost at API prices, not what a subscription charges.
The Conversation and This project groups each also give the average output rate across their runs, as "38 tok/s": every output token their runs reported over the time those runs spent waiting on the model, each run's time worked out as the task header's average is, as the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list)'s status says. Runs whose rate can't be worked out are left out of it, and where none can be, the figure is left out rather than shown as zero.

### Slice

Just left of the context figure sits the Slice toggle: a small ghost button with a scissors icon, reading "Slice", which shows as selected while it is on. It starts off. Its tooltip says what the prompt is sent as: while off, the prompt written as a spec, its references linking to the spec they name; while on, the prompt with the `piton slice` of each spec it references. Clicking it turns it on or off, and it applies to every tab, Ask included. It stays as it is across sends, tab switches, and project switches, as the prompt being written does, and the help text gives way to it as it does to the session controls.

### Model

Just left of the Slice toggle sits the model picker: a small ghost button reading the model the next prompt goes to, short, as "Opus", "Sonnet", or "Default", with a chevron, extra small and muted like the session controls. Clicking it opens a small menu above it listing the models the harness in use can be told, as the [HarnessIntegration](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says, the one chosen ticked, each with its full name muted beside it, and "Default" first, which tells the harness no model, so it uses its own. Picking one closes the menu and sends every prompt after it to that model, on every tab, Ask included, but Freeform, which passes the prompt to the harness as typed and is sent to the default; with Freeform selected the picker is disabled, its tooltip saying why. Its tooltip otherwise names the model chosen and says it applies to the next prompts sent.
The choice is remembered for the user, per harness, as the [UserPreferences](../../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences) says, and stays as it is across sends, tab switches, and project switches, as the Slice toggle does; it starts at Default. A prompt keeps the model it was sent with: its hidden anchor records it, so a queued prompt goes to the model chosen when it was queued, whatever is chosen when it is sent, and a resend goes to the model it was first sent to. A Chain prompt's steps all go to its model. A message sent to a running task goes to the model the task runs with, whatever is chosen. The help text gives way to it as it does to the session controls.
The models listed are those the harness can be told: for Claude Code, "Opus", "Sonnet", and "Haiku", given to it as `--model opus`, `--model sonnet`, or `--model haiku`; for Codex and OpenCode, the models their own configuration lists, given with `--model` or `-m` as each takes it. A model the harness refuses fails the run, saying so in the harness's own words. The notes, commit messages, and prompt titles keep their small model, whatever is chosen.

### Effort

Just left of the model picker sits the effort picker, laid out and behaving the same way: a small ghost button reading the reasoning effort the next prompt goes to, "Low", "Medium", "High", or "Default", with a chevron, which opens a menu of the levels the harness in use can be told, "Default" first, ticked when chosen, which tells the harness no effort, so it uses its own.
Only a harness that takes a reasoning effort offers it: Codex, told with `--model-reasoning-effort low`, `medium`, or `high`. Claude Code and OpenCode take no such setting, so with either in use the picker is disabled, its tooltip saying the harness in use has no effort levels to choose, and the next prompt goes without one.
It applies, is remembered, and travels with a prompt the same way the model picker does: on every tab but Freeform, which always goes without one; remembered for the user per harness, as the [UserPreferences](../../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences) says, starting at Default; a queued prompt, a resend, a Chain prompt's steps, and a message sent to a running task each keeping the effort they were first sent with; and the help text giving way to it as it does to the model picker. A level the harness refuses fails the run, saying so in the harness's own words. The notes, commit messages, and prompt titles are sent without an effort level, whatever is chosen.

### Colour

Queue and Preview are flat buttons on the theme's base surface, #444444 in dark mode, their labels in the theme's text colour, a step lighter on hover, doing what the send menu's options of those names do, with tooltips saying that Queue queues the prompt even while the harness is free, and that Preview previews the compiled prompt. They are offered just as the menu is: both are disabled while the input is empty, while a preview shows, and while a queued prompt is edited, and Queue is also disabled on the Ask tab, since a question never queues.
<Enter> allows for creating new lines, like Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it to the HarnessIntegration
Sending sends the prompt in the selected tab's mode, as the [PromptSending](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says. While the selected tab's lane is busy, as it says, the send button on the Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform tabs reads "Queue", since the prompt will queue: on Code while a task runs in the code lane, on Chain and Spec while one runs in the spec lane, and on Freeform while one runs in either, a Freeform task keeping both busy. Otherwise it reads "Send", so Spec reads "Send" while only a Code task runs. On the Ask tab it always reads "Send", because a question is never queued. The button is only disabled while the input is empty.
On the Code tab, while the send menu offers "Send to task", as its options say, the running task being a Code task in the code lane, the send button reads "Send to task" instead of "Queue", its tooltip saying it sends the prompt to the running task, and it and <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS) send to the task just as that option does, rather than queueing. The Queue button and the menu's "Queue" still queue the prompt. While the code lane is busy any other way, a Freeform task running, a Code task whose harness can't be fed more, a task building or compiling, or the previous tasks expanded over its output, the button reads "Queue" and the prompt queues, as ever. The Chain, Spec, Freeform, and Ask tabs never send to a task this way.

## Instructions

- [ChatInputInstruction](../../../shape/ChatInput.md#chat-input-instruction)

## Send Options

### Split Button

The send button is a split button: the send or queue button itself, and joined to its right, a narrow half with a chevron that opens a menu of other ways to send the prompt, above the button, its right edge lined up with the button's. The chevron half is disabled whenever the send half is, and while a preview shows, and its tooltip says it shows more ways to send, with its shortcut.

### Keyboard

<Ctrl+Shift+Enter> (<Cmd+Shift+Enter> on macOS) in the chat input opens the menu with its first option highlighted, and does nothing while the input is empty or a preview shows. While it is open, the text keeps focus, <Up> and <Down> move the highlight, wrapping around, <Enter> picks the highlighted option, and <Escape> closes the menu, as does pressing <Ctrl+Shift+Enter> again or the mouse anywhere outside it. Each option highlights on hover, and clicking one picks it.
## Tabs

The tabs along the top of the chat input, one for each mode.

### Overview

The input and buttons live inside the body of a tab bar, a flat strip 32 pixels tall on the ribbon's command area colour, #222222 in dark mode, with no line anywhere in it, whether beneath it, between its tabs, or around them. Each tab is only its label, in small text, with 8 pixels to each side of it and no border, and its label is always in its mode's colour at full strength, of the [PromptModes](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes), whether selected or not: Code red, Chain's icon purple, Spec blue, Ask green, and Freeform grey. The one exception is Chain selected, when Code and Spec take Chain's purple too, as the chain says. The selected tab is marked only by its background, the same surface as the body beneath it, so it reads as a tab joined to that body; unselected tabs have none, and show the strip, lightening a little on hover. There is a tab for each of the [PromptModes](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes), in their order: Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, and Freeform. Code, Spec, Ask, and Freeform are ordinary tabs. Chain is also a tab, just a small one, because it only shows an icon. All five sit flush against each other with no extra gaps, and no tab has more padding than a normal tab.
The chat input starts in the combined mode: Chain is selected, so Code and Spec are selected together, and a prompt sent before switching tabs changes the code and the spec together. Each open project keeps the tab it was left on, as the [OpenProjects](../../open-projects/index.md#open-projects) says, so a project starts on Chain the first time it is opened in a launch, and switching back to it selects the tab it was on.
Pressing <Ctrl+Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to Chain to Spec to Ask to Freeform and back to Code, <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> the other way, and focus remains in the chat input. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.
<Tab> and <Shift+Tab> don't switch tabs, and don't indent the text either. They move keyboard focus out of the chat input to the next or previous control, as they do everywhere else. While the completion menu is open, <Tab> is still the menu's.

### Chain

Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it selects both Code and Spec. Its icon is drawn in Chain's colour, the purple of the [PromptModes](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes), selected or not, as every tab's label is in its mode's colour. It never shows a focus outline, and its icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two is selected.
Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of them.
Chain, like every tab, has no line along its bottom or sides, in combined mode or separate, since the tab bar draws no lines at all. Nothing draws a line beneath Chain and then hides it, since a hidden line can show again wherever rounding to the display's pixels uncovers it.
Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both. Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected, Code and Spec both show as selected, one continuous background beneath the two of them and Chain, reading as a single unified tab. Chain itself has a transparent background, so the joined Code and Spec show through underneath it.
While Chain is selected, the Code and Spec labels are drawn in Chain's purple, the same colour as its icon, rather than red and blue, so the unified tab reads as one mode in one colour. Their colour follows the slide: as Code and Spec slide together, their labels shift from red and blue to purple, and as they slide apart they shift back, each reaching its own colour as the tabs settle.

### Help

To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.
It reads what the selected tab's mode is for, as the [PromptModes](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes) says.

### Session

At the far right of the bar, at the right end of the help text, sits how much context the selected tab's conversation holds, then a New conversation button. Each lane's tasks, and the questions of the Ask tab, have a conversation of their own, as the [HarnessIntegration](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says, so the figure is the spec lane's on the Spec and Chain tabs, a Chain prompt starting in the spec lane, the code lane's on Code and Freeform, and the questions' on Ask.
The figure reads "Context", then the number of tokens, short and extra small, muted: "850", "42.1k", "123k", or "1.2M", to a decimal place below a hundred of a unit. It follows each reply as the harness reports it. While the next prompt would start a new conversation, as when the project has none yet or New conversation was just pressed, it reads "Context 0". Its tooltip says how many tokens the conversation the next prompt carries on holds, or that the next prompt starts a new conversation.
New conversation is a small ghost button with a sparkles icon, reading "New conversation". Pressing it starts a new conversation for the selected tab: the spec lane's on Spec, the code lane's on Code and Freeform, both lanes' on Chain, whose steps run in both, and the questions' on Ask. The next run of that conversation, from any tab sharing it, starts a new one with no context instead of carrying on, and the figure reads "Context 0". A run of the conversation left that is still going finishes as it would, but neither it nor the project's history brings that conversation back, even once the project is closed and opened again, as the [HarnessIntegration](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says.
It can be pressed while a run in that conversation is under way, a task on Code, Chain, Spec, or Freeform, or any question on Ask, without waiting for it to finish. Pressed while a task runs, the prompts sent meanwhile queue or run as ever, and the next task of the lane reset to start, whether sent straight away or from the queue, starts a new conversation with no context, the ones after it carrying that one on. That holds even when the running task is the first of its conversation and the harness hasn't yet said which conversation it is: once it does, it isn't carried on either.
Whether a task starts a new conversation is part of its prompt, recorded in its hidden anchor. Pressed for a lane with prompts queued, New conversation marks the first in that lane's queue, saving it again with the project, so it still starts the new conversation once the project is closed and opened again. With nothing queued, the next task sent or queued takes the mark. Cancelling the marked prompt passes the mark on to the one that now comes first, or, with nothing left queued, to the next task sent or queued. A task marked this way never carries on the conversation before it when it runs.
<Ctrl+N> while in the chat input does just what pressing New conversation does, for the selected tab, and nothing while the button is disabled. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.
Its tooltip says which conversation it resets, with its shortcut: "Start a new conversation for spec tasks (Ctrl+N)", "Start a new conversation for code tasks (Ctrl+N)", "Start a new conversation for spec and code tasks (Ctrl+N)", or "Start a new conversation for questions (Ctrl+N)", adding, while a run in it is under way, that the run finishes in the conversation left. It is disabled only while that conversation has nothing to carry on and no run in it is under way, its tooltip then saying the next task, or question, already starts a new conversation.
Both sit on the bar's bottom line, which runs beneath them as it does beneath the help text, and neither is cut off: the help text gives way to them when the bar is narrow.

### Usage

Just right of the context figure, before New conversation, sits the agent's usage: how much of the harness picked, of the [HarnessIntegration](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration), has been used, as Claude Code's /usage shows it. Its summary is short and extra small, muted like the context figure: "Usage", then the share used of the plan limit nearest to running out, such as "Usage 42%", turning the theme's warning colour from 80% and its error colour once the limit is reached. When the harness reports no plan limits, the summary is what this project's runs would cost at API prices, as below, such as "Usage $1.24", or the tokens they used, as the context figure is written, when no cost can be worked out. Until anything has been reported, it reads "Usage", with nothing after it.
Clicking the summary opens a popover above it with all the details, each group headed, and each figure labelled:
- Plan limits: each limit the harness reports, such as the current
  session's and the week's, with the share used as a bar and a
  percentage, and when it resets.
- Conversation: the context the selected tab's conversation holds,
  and its input, output, cache-read, and cache-written tokens, and
  what they would cost at API prices.
- This project: every run the project has made, as below, split
  into tasks and questions, with its tokens by model and what
  they would cost at API prices.
- The harness and model the figures came from, and when they were
  last reported.
The popover is laid out in two columns side by side, with a gap of 16 pixels between them and a thin line in the theme's line colour down the middle. The left column holds what is going on now: Plan limits, then Conversation, then, at its foot, the harness and model the figures came from. The right column holds This project, which is the longest: Tasks and Questions, then the tokens by model, then its cost with its breakdown and the note about API prices. Each column is as tall as its own groups, both starting at the top, and the popover is as tall as the taller of them. Each column is at least 240 pixels wide, so the popover is about twice as wide as it was as one column, but never wider than the window less 16 pixels each side; where the window is too narrow for both, the right column goes beneath the left, as one column again, with no line between them. A column whose groups are all left out is not shown, and the other is the popover's only column; when nothing has been reported at all, the popover is a single column saying so. Within each column, each figure is a row, its label at the left and its value right-aligned in tabular figures. The popover scrolls as a whole, not each column on its own, when it is taller than the room above the summary.
A group, or a figure, the harness doesn't report is left out rather than shown as zero, and when nothing has been reported the popover says so. The figures come from what the harness reports as its runs go, and from what it reported for the runs saved in the project, never from running anything of its own to ask, and update in place while the popover is open, following each reply. Clicking outside the popover, or pressing Escape, closes it. The summary's tooltip says to click for the details. Like the context figure, it is never cut off: the help text gives way to it.
A run's own usage is never the figures its result reports as they stand. Claude Code's result reports its `modelUsage` and `total_cost_usd` as running totals for the whole conversation, so a run that carries on a conversation includes every run before it in that conversation. A run's own figures are how much its conversation's totals rose since that conversation's previous run, each model's tokens apart; a run that carries on a copy of a conversation, as a question asked while another runs does, is measured from the run whose conversation it copied. When the totals went down instead, any of them, the conversation started over, and the run counts in full, as does the first run of a conversation. Runs are taken in the order they were sent, whether they were saved in the history or have just reported, so every run is counted once and no run's figures are counted again in a later one's.
This project covers every run saved with the project, every task in its history, each step of a chain counted as a run of its own, and every question in its asks, not only those since it was opened, worked out from what the harness printed for each, as its record keeps it. It keeps updating as new runs report, each run counted once it reports, and a run under way not yet counted. It is split into Tasks and Questions, each giving how many runs there were and, beside it, muted, how many of them reported no usage, such as "42 runs · 3 without usage", the latter left out when none. Beneath them, for each model the runs used, by name, its input, output, cache-read, and cache-written tokens, as the context figure writes them, across tasks and questions together.
Cost is worked out from the tokens, at each model's published API prices per million tokens, which the application keeps for the models it knows: input, output, cache reads, and cache writes, at the 5-minute rate or the 1-hour rate, using the split between them the harness reports. Cache writes it reports no split for are priced at the 5-minute rate. A model is matched by its id, whatever date or context-size suffix it carries. The cost the harness reports itself, such as `total_cost_usd`, is never used. A model whose prices aren't known gets no cost, never a guess: its tokens are still shown, it is marked "Price unknown", and the totals that leave it out say so beside them. The project's cost is shown as a total, and beneath it how much of it was input, output, cache reads, and cache writes, each in dollars and as a share of the total, since caching is most of it. Beneath the cost, muted, it says this is what the tokens would cost at API prices, not what a subscription charges.
The Conversation and This project groups each also give the average output rate across their runs, as "38 tok/s": every output token their runs reported over the time those runs spent waiting on the model, each run's time worked out as the task header's average is, as the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list)'s status says. Runs whose rate can't be worked out are left out of it, and where none can be, the figure is left out rather than shown as zero.

### Slice

Just left of the context figure sits the Slice toggle: a small ghost button with a scissors icon, reading "Slice", which shows as selected while it is on. It starts off. Its tooltip says what the prompt is sent as: while off, the prompt written as a spec, its references linking to the spec they name; while on, the prompt with the `piton slice` of each spec it references. Clicking it turns it on or off, and it applies to every tab, Ask included. It stays as it is across sends, tab switches, and project switches, as the prompt being written does, and the help text gives way to it as it does to the session controls.

### Model

Just left of the Slice toggle sits the model picker: a small ghost button reading the model the next prompt goes to, short, as "Opus", "Sonnet", or "Default", with a chevron, extra small and muted like the session controls. Clicking it opens a small menu above it listing the models the harness in use can be told, as the [HarnessIntegration](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says, the one chosen ticked, each with its full name muted beside it, and "Default" first, which tells the harness no model, so it uses its own. Picking one closes the menu and sends every prompt after it to that model, on every tab, Ask included, but Freeform, which passes the prompt to the harness as typed and is sent to the default; with Freeform selected the picker is disabled, its tooltip saying why. Its tooltip otherwise names the model chosen and says it applies to the next prompts sent.
The choice is remembered for the user, per harness, as the [UserPreferences](../../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences) says, and stays as it is across sends, tab switches, and project switches, as the Slice toggle does; it starts at Default. A prompt keeps the model it was sent with: its hidden anchor records it, so a queued prompt goes to the model chosen when it was queued, whatever is chosen when it is sent, and a resend goes to the model it was first sent to. A Chain prompt's steps all go to its model. A message sent to a running task goes to the model the task runs with, whatever is chosen. The help text gives way to it as it does to the session controls.
The models listed are those the harness can be told: for Claude Code, "Opus", "Sonnet", and "Haiku", given to it as `--model opus`, `--model sonnet`, or `--model haiku`; for Codex and OpenCode, the models their own configuration lists, given with `--model` or `-m` as each takes it. A model the harness refuses fails the run, saying so in the harness's own words. The notes, commit messages, and prompt titles keep their small model, whatever is chosen.

### Effort

Just left of the model picker sits the effort picker, laid out and behaving the same way: a small ghost button reading the reasoning effort the next prompt goes to, "Low", "Medium", "High", or "Default", with a chevron, which opens a menu of the levels the harness in use can be told, "Default" first, ticked when chosen, which tells the harness no effort, so it uses its own.
Only a harness that takes a reasoning effort offers it: Codex, told with `--model-reasoning-effort low`, `medium`, or `high`. Claude Code and OpenCode take no such setting, so with either in use the picker is disabled, its tooltip saying the harness in use has no effort levels to choose, and the next prompt goes without one.
It applies, is remembered, and travels with a prompt the same way the model picker does: on every tab but Freeform, which always goes without one; remembered for the user per harness, as the [UserPreferences](../../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences) says, starting at Default; a queued prompt, a resend, a Chain prompt's steps, and a message sent to a running task each keeping the effort they were first sent with; and the help text giving way to it as it does to the model picker. A level the harness refuses fails the run, saying so in the harness's own words. The notes, commit messages, and prompt titles are sent without an effort level, whatever is chosen.

content.text:
I read the screenshot as two problems and changed the chat input spec to fix both. You didn't say exactly what was wrong, so tell me if you meant something else. `piton check` and `piton build` both pass.

**The control row overflows.** When the chat input is narrow, the row with the tabs and controls runs past its right edge. Slice, Context, Usage and New conversation end up drawn over the empty area beside it. The spec said these controls are "never cut off" but didn't say what happens once the help text has made all the room it can.

**The send button's label is cut off.** It reads "Que…" because the button column was a fixed 88 pixels.

**What changed in the spec:**
- **New "Fit" rule** (Tabs, `#fit`): the row is exactly as wide as the chat input and nothing in it goes past the input's edge, overlaps another control, or is clipped mid-label. As the input narrows, the row makes room in this order:
  1. The help text is cut off, then left out.
  2. New conversation and Slice show only their icons. Context and Usage show only their numbers. Each keeps its full wording in its tooltip.
  3. The controls move onto a second line under the tabs, aligned right.

  The tabs themselves never shrink. Widening the input reverses the steps.
- **Button column** (`#description`): at least 88 pixels, and wide enough for the longest label, "Send to task", with its icon and dropdown chevron. Its width doesn't change when the label does, no label is cut off with "…", and the text box takes the remaining room.

The code should follow `.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#fit` and `#description`.
